item.title: C.E.O.s Say the A.I. Rollout Is Going Well. Employees Feel Differently.
item.description:
By Jordyn Holman

When it comes to artificial intelligence, chief executives and their work forces aren’t seeing eye to eye.

Corporate leaders, increasingly in earnings calls and interviews, tout productivity gains and say they are doing right by their workers as they roll out the technology.

But workers are much more concerned about being supplanted, and they don’t trust their company’s executives.

A survey from the Milken Institute-Harris Poll Listening Project recently found that more than two-thirds of business leaders expect they will be better off financially in five years because of A.I., while just 27 percent of the U.S. work force felt the same way — a whopping 41 point gap.

Workers also see less A.I. transformation than leadership does. Nearly three-fourths of leaders say A.I. has significantly changed the way work is done, compared with 58 percent of entry and midlevel employees, according to a report released this month from the Wharton School.

“We have corner offices and cubicles, driving the same economy, but living in completely different realities,” John Gerzema, C.E.O. of the Harris Poll, said in an email. “There is a gulf in hope between what leaders think A.I. could bring to companies and what employees feel it is taking away from them.”

What might be worse is that C.E.O.s don’t seem to recognize the disconnect, or that they’re losing the trust of their workers.

For example: Just 15 percent of C.E.O.s said they were concerned about how their approach to A.I. could erode their employees’ trust, according to a survey released this month by consultancy BCG. But 40 percent of workers said their C.E.O. has not been transparent enough about the impact of A.I. on their role and career trajectory.

The distrust doesn’t make for a successful transformation, said Julia Dhar, the leader of the North American people and organization practice at BCG and an author of the study.

“You will not get the people you need to start using it more intensively to do so,” Dhar said. “And there is a very good chance you will get backsliding or regression from other people.”

Hemant Taneja, who leads the venture capital firm General Catalyst, said the findings of the BCG report were not surprising, but relatable.

“When there’s more ambiguity, you need to over-communicate,” Taneja said in an interview. “I’m feeling the pain of that in my own business as well.”

He said he has been working to build trust by explaining his decisions around A.I. to employees and founders, especially when they change.

“You have to be vulnerable about the fact that we don’t have all the answers,” Taneja said. “We directionally know where to go, but we don’t know all the answers, and so it’s OK to change assumptions and change your mind.” Dhar said one C.E.O. she knows starts frank discussions around A.I. by asking his frontline employees, “What is the silliest thing we do at this company?” This approach works, she said, because it’s not judgmental, and the C.E.O. doesn’t have to agree on it or make a promise to look into it further.

“But you’ve given people a really easy way to make their voice heard,” she said.

Tim Walsh, chief executive of consultancy KPMG, says when he travels to offices in different cities he makes a point to sit down with both the partners in the business as well as employees.

“I need to understand how they’re feeling, I need to understand how the technology is being received and I need to understand their concerns,” Walsh said in an interview. “I will tell you it’s hard to get it at my level.”

Walsh said he hasn’t mastered the art of getting rank-and-file employees to open up completely in front of him. KPMG relies on anonymous employee surveys as a platform where more junior employees can feel freer to complain.

Despite a struggle to build trust with workers around A.I., there is a bright spot for chief executives. The distrust Americans have toward C.E.O.s and more specifically their own C.E.O. is less than it is for other institutions in American life like media outlets, NGOs and government, according to the Edelman Trust Barometer, which has been measuring trust levels in for the past 26 years.

The research also found that U.S. employees appreciated hearing from their leaders about A.I. even in instances when they didn’t have all the answers.

“People are often very realistic about a business reality and their requests are often quite humble,” Dhar said. “They say, I would just hope the leaders are able to be honest and specific about the changes that we are making and the reason behind them.”

Tesla and SpaceX are considering a merger. Elon Musk confirmed on Tuesday that the boards of each company have formed a special committee to explore a tie-up. Musk cautioned that any such proposal would require approval from at least 50 percent of all outstanding shares in Tesla.

Researchers discovered a widespread security vulnerability. Companies and government agencies scrambled to patch the major bug in PHP, an open-source programming language that is critical to internet architecture. The vulnerability was detected with the help of A.I., but bad actors could also use A.I. to exploit it.

Mark Zuckerberg struck a deal to pay California’s potential billionaire tax. Zuckerberg negotiated with the company’s board over how he would pay the one-time 5 percent tax on all holdings. Meta responded by creating a new class of shares that allows him to raise billions without compromising his voting power in the company. In return, he agreed to stay in the state for eight more years, except for under some conditions. The new share class will also let Meta raise more money for its A.I. ambitions.

More big deals: Saudi Arabia postponed its big investment conference amid concerns about security. Trump asked Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the Starshield satellite communications network. And next week will be a big test for the strength of A.I. financing: Anthropic is expected to file its public I.P.O. prospectus within the next few days, and Google, Microsoft and Amazon report earnings.

Meta’s new A.I. team has 50 engineers for every manager. Airbnb’s C.E.O., Brian Chesky, has popularized the delegation-shunning strategy of staying in “founders mode.” While Uber, Meta, Amazon and more have been aggressively laying off middle managers.

In the midst of what has been termed “the Great Flattening,” hierarchy seems to have few defenders. But Nir Halevy, a professor of organizational behavior at Stanford University, argues that levels of management are actually quite useful — when done right. He talked with Sarah Kessler about his new book, “Level Up.” The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

Why don’t flat organizations work?

It’s difficult to scale. And we all engage in social comparisons. Those tendencies don’t disappear just because we decided to create a flat structure.

There’s a lot of evidence showing that informal hierarchies are very swift and powerful in the tendency to emerge.

What do you want instead of an informal hierarchy?

You want it to be based on common values. We want to create a hierarchy that provides people with multiple pathways to contribute and thrive and ascend and lead.

What usually makes the hierarchy dysfunctional?

One, if they’re ultracompetitive. And that competition might manifest in withholding help or may actually lead to sabotage.

Broken hierarchies are unjust. You really deserve a promotion, but you’re not going to get the promotion because the boss’s nephew got it. You get arbitrary decisions that are not justified and not explained.

And instability. You will experience a lot of unpredictable, swift changes. People leave, there is a lot of turnover, retention becomes a struggle and people feel a sense of threat and stress and paranoia.

Is there a size at which you don’t need hierarchy?

One of the examples I discuss in the book is Valve, which makes video games and has a few hundred employees. It presents itself to the world as a flat organization. If you go to their landing page, they say, We’ve been boss free since 1996. But they do distinguish based on salaries. They are not all receiving the same information. They have informal hierarchies.

But if I have just like 10 people, is it reasonable to say I’m the boss, but everybody else is on the same level?

You can say that. The question is the extent to which the people actually think that it’s true or fair.

Does A.I. change hierarchy? Do we still need middle management?

Initiatives to use technology to flatten organizations are definitely on the rise. But there is a neglect of the multiple functions that people, let’s say middle management, are doing.

If people erroneously believe their managers are only aggregating information from the bottom, transferring it upward, or taking kind of directions from the top and transferring it downward, then they might mistakenly believe that A.I. can replace employees.

This question comes from a recent edition of the newsletter. Click an answer to see if you’re right. (The link is free.)

A.I. music is flooding onto music streaming platforms. Which of the following listening services bans it?

Bandcamp

Apple Music

Spotify

All of the above

Thanks for reading! We’ll see you Monday.

We’d like your feedback. Please email thoughts and suggestions to dealbook@nytimes.com.

item.title: A Song in Your Heart and a Pillow Under Your Head: 5 Hotels for Music Lovers
item.description:
Music lovers have long been willing to travel to see their favorite acts, and in turn hotels have played up their proximity to concert venues. These days, more hotels are striving to become music destinations in their own right. Some are themed, like Dolly Parton’s new SongTeller Hotel in Nashville, Tenn. Others are providing instrument lessons, listening rooms, recording studios, D.J. residencies and on-site concert series, be it at design hotels (like the Parker Palm Springs, which this month began offering Parker Sessions in a new amphitheater) or at major chains such as W, Virgin, Hard Rock and Sonesta International.

Below are some of the latest spots where music is at the heart of the hotel’s character. Whether you’re interested in rock, jazz, blues or electronic music, these getaways aim to put a song in your heart and a pillow under your head.

San Antonio, Texas

This over-100-year-old hotel in downtown San Antonio — where in 1936 the blues musician Robert Johnson made one of his rare recordings — has reopened after a $70 million renovation. Big band musicians, including Alphonse Trent, Mack Rogers and Henry Lange, once led the in-house orchestras, and while the Beaux-Arts-influenced hotel has been updated with reimagined spaces and new dining concepts (it also joined Marriott’s Tribute Portfolio), its musical ties remain. All of its 311 rooms and suites have record players, along with a copy of a Johnson album. A vinyl library with more than 1,000 records allows you to check out your favorite.

Regular performances, be it mariachi or country music, are part of the experience. On Wednesdays, stop by the new Studio Lounge Sessions music series, where a lead artist typically invites friends to make music together. Bar 414 (named for the room number where Johnson recorded) offers free live music (the schedule is here). And the Crystal Ballroom has ticketed concerts on special occasions.

From Nov. 12 to 14, there will be a celebration of the 90th anniversary of the Johnson recordings featuring his grandson, Steven Johnson, and performances by artists, including the pedal-steel guitarist Robert Randolph. Ally Venable, Tomar & the FCs and Nicky Diamonds will also perform, and there will be tours of the hotel’s new recording studio.

In addition to Bar 414, you’ll find three other places to grab a bite. Prices from $250 a night; see the website for packages and offers.

Wanship, Utah

When the luxury hospitality group Auberge Collection began noticing traveler interest in music tourism, it created its own concert series, featuring performances in intimate settings. At the Lodge at Blue Sky, a 46-room-and-suite getaway set on a 4,000-acre private ranch in the Wasatch Mountain Range, about half an hour from Park City, upcoming performances include HARDY (Nov. 21) and Maren Morris (Dec. 4).

In addition to attending concerts in what was once the property’s indoor riding arena, you can go hiking, mountain biking, horseback riding, snowshoeing or try a massage, yoga or guided meditation. Yuta, the main restaurant, serves regional cuisine, including Utah rib-eye and lamb rack, and organic produce from the lodge’s farm.

Accommodations have picturesque views and include suites, many with outdoor fireplaces. Room prices are from $1,800 a night. Packages and à la carte concert ticket options and prices vary by artist. The Auberge Concert Series schedule, including seat details and pricing, is at Auberge.com/music.

New York

This 201-room-and-suite hotel in Midtown Manhattan is home to a new 1940s-and-’50s-inspired jazz club with 170 seats. Known as the Pocket, the club is a nod to the jazz rooms that populated 52nd Street in that era. On any given night, amid the green leather banquettes, cherry wood and the 1964 Steinway grand piano, you might hear jazz, Latin music, hip-hop, R&B or soul.

Musicians scheduled to perform in November include Grammy Award winners such as Mingus Big Band, Arturo O’Farrill & the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra, and the New Orleans-based Dirty Dozen Brass Band. Complement the music with a martini or an Old Fashioned, and order from a menu that includes starters like broiled oysters in various styles; entrees such as prime rib, roasted chicken, fish or “broccoli steak”; and for dessert, pies from the Four & Twenty Blackbirds bakery, including salted caramel apple crumb and rhubarb crumble.

After the show, retire to your graphic black-and-white room (some rooms have outdoor space). Prices from $299 a night. For the latest performance schedule and ticket information visit thepocketnyc.com/calendar.

Madrid; London; Tulum, Mexico

UMusic Hotels are a remix of traditional hotels, places to both sleep and enjoy live events. In December, UMusic Hotel Denmark Street is scheduled to open in London’s Soho neighborhood, named for the street that’s long been associated with the British music business and musicians like Elton John and the Sex Pistols. The Lower Third, a live music venue (and the name of a band David Bowie once worked with), is on Denmark Street, while the 2,000-seat music and performance venue, Outernet Live, is close by. The new 26-room-and-suite hotel will include a lobby cocktail bar and a fitness room, and will sit in the midst of the action.

Also in December, the brand plans to open UMusic Hotel & Beach Club Tulum, with 57 rooms and villas (some with Jacuzzis or private pools) and a beach club. The property is being designed as a destination for live music and other events, and will have recording studios and production facilities as well as beach access and a pool.

UMusic Hotels is developing properties in Kansas City and Austin as well, but in the meantime you can check out the first of its hotels, UMusic Hotel Madrid, which is near Plaza Mayor and has 130 rooms and suites, and access to the Teatro Albéniz from the hotel lobby. The hotel also has a vinyl library and a piano bar. Prices from €350 a night.

Paris

In 1965, a nightclub called Bus Palladium opened in the capital’s Pigalle district, attracting revelers like Serge Gainsbourg, David Bowie and the Rolling Stones. Today, that nightclub has been reimagined as a five-story boutique hotel with a subterranean club where Madonna and Charli XCX have performed.

Designed by Karl Fournier and Olivier Marty, co-founders of the Paris-based architecture firm Studio KO, the hotel has 35 rooms and suites that mix elements of Brutalism, like raw concrete ceilings, with pink carpets and Hollywood-style mirrors. You can listen to playlists created by Caroline de Maigret, the French model and music producer, who is also the artistic director of the hotel, on OJAS speakers. There’s a playlist called “Boogie Nights” for when you’re getting ready to go out, with music by Prince and Grace Jones, and another called (naturally) “the French Connection,” dedicated to French music with songs by Jacqueline Taïeb and La Femme. Even little things nod to music, like light switches meant to look like vintage amplifiers.

Slide into a red velvet booth for dinner by the French chef Valentin Raffali at the hotel’s evocative restaurant, which has a wall of vinyl records, including those that belonged to Bus Palladium’s founder, James Arch. Sip a cocktail at the bar before heading to the club, where you can dance until the wee hours beneath a disco ball. The hotel, part of the Chapitre Six collection of French hotels, has prices from around €490, or about $550, a night.

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

item.title: What’s Riding on Anthropic’s Market Debut? Nearly Everything.
item.description:
When Anthropic goes public as soon as next month, its initial offering will be more than just a coming-out party for the artificial intelligence company. It will also be a litmus test for the economy, with trillions of dollars at stake.

Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, is a tent pole of the A.I. industry. Valued in the private markets at nearly $1 trillion and backed by more than $130 billion in funding, it could raise $100 billion in its offering and promptly become one of the world’s biggest public companies. But the stakes are even higher than that.

Anthropic and OpenAI, its chief rival, sit atop a pyramid of business partners and suppliers — infrastructure providers, chipmakers, energy companies and A.I. start-ups — that have all spent heavily over the last four years because they believe demand for A.I. products will keep growing.

Anthropic’s listing will provide the first in-depth look at the health of a key business underlying the A.I. boom — and will be a test of its durability. Is there unending appetite for A.I. services to justify the spending on chips, data centers and other infrastructure? Or will Anthropic’s performance show that there are limits?

“For the market, it’s a bellwether,” said Umesh Padval, an investor at Seligman Ventures, who has worked in tech for nearly 40 years.

If Anthropic disappoints in its public debut, that could hurt investor confidence and cascade into a wider market sell-off, casting doubts on how much longer the A.I. boom can go. A successful offering could lift the market and pave the way for more A.I. companies to go public.

Stock markets are already on edge, with technology stocks broadly falling this month, led by a sell-off in the companies that design and produce the computer chips that power A.I. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is in a bear market, defined as a decline of 20 percent or more from a recent high and a sign of significant investor angst, after falling 26 percent from its June peak.

Over the last couple of weeks, Microsoft canceled a deal with Nscale, a provider of data centers. A report from the research firm Gartner predicted that 80 percent of “neoclouds,” the companies that provide data and computing power for A.I. firms, could be forced out of business. And Ken Griffin, the billionaire owner of the hedge fund Citadel, said A.I. investors were “almost certainly” in a bubble.

Those negative signals have added to fears about the huge piles of money being spent on A.I. infrastructure. Amazon, Meta, Google and Microsoft have said they plan to spend at least $740 billion on A.I. infrastructure, including data centers, this year. Private market investors have poured $1.1 trillion into Anthropic, OpenAI and other A.I. companies since 2022, according to PitchBook, which tracks investments.

As spending and investment have risen in private markets, public investments have grown, too, increasing the stock market’s reliance on the performance of the A.I. industry. The top 10 stocks in the S&P 500 are worth more than $1 trillion together, with eight of them being tech companies. Combined, the top 10 account for over 40 percent of the index, up from less than 20 percent a decade ago.

When Anthropic is added to the index, it is likely to displace either Berkshire Hathaway or Eli Lilly, the only non-tech companies with valuations above $1 trillion, from the top 10.

“There is a lot riding on this one,” said Brad Gastwirth, the global head of research and market intelligence at Circular Technology, a supply chain services firm. “If it goes bad, it’s going to bring down the market.”

This month, Anthropic gathered investors at its San Francisco headquarters to present its financial performance and growth plans. By most measures, its numbers were astounding. The company’s revenue hit $16.8 billion in the third quarter, up 45 percent from the prior quarter. But investors compared that with even faster growth of 141 percent in the second quarter.

How Anthropic explains that slowdown will be important. If it was because the company lost market share to OpenAI or companies using cheaper open-source A.I. models — the technology that powers chatbots and other tools that generate videos, text and computer code — that means the overall demand for A.I. services remains healthy. If Anthropic’s growth slowed because the entire market saw less demand for A.I. products, the reaction could be more dramatic.

Anthropic declined to comment. (The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

For the past year, Anthropic has been Silicon Valley’s hottest company, thanks partly to Claude Code, the service that transformed how software engineers write code. The company’s revenue soared, causing private market investors to drive up its valuation to $965 billion, topping OpenAI.

To meet the demand for its A.I. products, Anthropic struck deals worth hundreds of billions to lease computing power from Google, Amazon and Microsoft. It has also spent on chips from Nvidia and data centers from Nscale and others. The companies serving Anthropic are, in turn, shelling out money to their suppliers.

But over the summer, some Anthropic customers concluded they were spending too much on “tokens,” or units of data processed and generated by A.I. systems. They sought cheaper options. Meta, one of Anthropic’s largest customers, projected this year that it would spend as much as $10 billion a year on the company’s technology, but pulled back as it switched to other A.I. models.

Stocks of some A.I. companies that went public this year have wilted. Shares of Cerebras, a Silicon Valley maker of A.I. chips, have fallen roughly 40 percent from their offering price in May. Shares of Accelevation, an A.I. infrastructure company, are trading about a third lower than their $18 offering price in September. Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which went public in June, has also fallen far from its peak, though it remains roughly 9 percent above its offering price.

Against this backdrop, the market for initial public offerings has slowed. Holtec, which provides nuclear energy to the A.I. sector, withdrew its listing last month. SB Energy, a data center company controlled by SoftBank, one of OpenAI’s biggest backers, and Aggreko, a power company that works with data centers, have delayed their plans to go public.

A.I. infrastructure is a “dominant theme” of the I.P.O. market this year, said Matthew Kennedy, a senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, which tracks public listings. “It’s also been among the hardest hit by the sell-off these past few weeks.”

Bankers have warned companies that they may not get the valuations they were contemplating just two months ago. In an earnings call this month, David Solomon, the chief executive of Goldman Sachs, said that while the market for public offerings was “wide open,” companies seeking valuations close to those discussed this summer might choose to wait.

“Things got a little bit softer in September,” he said.

Anthropic’s revenue numbers have added to the doubts. The company had been expected to go public at a valuation as high as $2 trillion. But after seeing the slowing growth and the market doldrums, some investors have started discussing a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $1.7 trillion, according to one person with knowledge of the matter.

A.I. executives have been trying to provide reassurance. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, which supplies chips to the A.I. sector, saw “no ceiling” to its profits, its chief executive, C.C. Wei, said this month.

Late last week, amid growing concerns about A.I. spending, the markets fell further. The tech-heavy Nasdaq experienced its largest drop since June.

Sri Muppidi contributed reporting from San Francisco, and Joe Rennison from New York.

item.title: Why Musk Is Predicting ‘Guppy-Level Death’ for Scores of A.I. Companies
item.description:
Andrew here. Just in: Apollo Global Management is said to be nearing a deal to buy a nearly 10 percent stake in Mubadala Capital, the asset management arm of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth fund and the majority owner of Fortress Investment Group, CNBC reports, citing unnamed sources.

Elon Musk was busy this weekend. He warned that interest rate increases were going to crush independent data centers, which is already rattling neocloud stocks. Plus, the top law firm Weil Gotshal & Manges is dealing with a messy wave of defections that has people wondering what’s next for it. More below.

Concerns about rampant artificial intelligence spending have slowed the stock market rally and driven up tech companies’ borrowing costs. Now Elon Musk predicts that many companies tied to the A.I. boom will not survive, as they’ve been effectively shut out of the debt market.

The ominous remarks on social media have come as investors brace for a major test this week. More hyperscalers’ earnings are on tap, and details on Anthropic’s upcoming I.P.O. may be, too.

Could a looming credit bottleneck wipe out a slew of tech companies? Musk thinks so. But he said his $2 trillion company, SpaceX, was well cushioned thanks to its investment-grade credit status and booming Starlink internet business.

He underscored that point on Sunday by announcing that SpaceX had just landed a $40 billion debt deal to buy more chips, including from Nvidia. But that may not be final.

Who’s at risk? Musk singled out neoclouds, the companies that sell computing power to A.I. companies. Many of them, he wrote on social media, face “guppy-level death and consolidation.”

Bears may seize on Musk’s warning. Nasdaq futures point to a modest rebound on Monday, but investors have punished neoclouds lately. For example, shares in CoreWeave, which counts Anthropic and Microsoft as customers, were sold off sharply last week and are down again in premarket trading. CoreWeave’s credit default swaps, a measure of credit risk, have ballooned, too, as investors worry about the borrowing binge driving the A.I. build-out.

But Musk’s comments need context. Bloomberg, citing unnamed sources, reports that the $40 billion credit line for SpaceX that Musk referred to is not a done deal. It’s worth noting that SpaceX, which competes with neoclouds to sell computing capacity to A.I. companies, has also seen its credit costs soar, Bloomberg adds, even as its A.I. revenues climb.

Watch Anthropic, which is expected to go public as soon as next month. Investors are eagerly anticipating that it will file the paperwork for its I.P.O. any day now. Details have been leaking for weeks. Still, there are big questions about its key customers and major risks, be they financial — it pays billions to SpaceX, Amazon and Google, among others, for cloud and computing capacity — or societal.

Wall Street is hoping a strong trading debut from Anthropic will allay many of the fears about the A.I. bubble that have gripped the market narrative recently. And Meta on Monday announced it would seek to raise approximately $35 billion in a new share offering and $60 billion in the future to help pay for its huge A.I. expenditures.

More Musk news: The tech mogul this weekend gave his first explanation about the throttling of Ukraine’s access to Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite communications network. After President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said the service had been restored, Musk admitted SpaceX had slowed the service and accused Ukraine’s military of violating Starlink’s terms of service by using the network for offensive drone strikes. Ukraine disputed the claim.

Calls are growing from both parties for Musk to be investigated over the slowdown. Robert Reich, the former labor secretary, argued on his podcast this weekend that Democrats should go further, to “defund Musk” and lay “the groundwork for nationalizing” Starlink and SpaceX.

Brazilians re-elect Lula. The country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, defied the odds, beating Flávio Bolsonaro in a runoff election on Sunday. (Bolsonaro, a right-wing politician who drew support from President Trump, has asked for the election to be annulled because voting was extended for two hours.) Lula’s standing up to Trump and to American tech giants appears to have paid off politically, but the Brazilian market is expected to fall on Monday as investors worry about his handling of inflation and soaring debt.

Central banks and earnings take center stage. Market watchers expect the Fed, the European Central Bank and the Bank of Japan to hold interest rates steady at their respective meetings on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Traders will be focused on hyperscalers’ capital expenditure plans this week as the chipmaker SK Hynix reports results on Tuesday, Alphabet and Microsoft go on Wednesday and Amazon publishes its numbers on Thursday. Also, Israel is holding elections on Tuesday.

The airport partially reopens in the Saudi capital. The Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen claimed on Sunday that it had attacked the international airport in Riyadh hours after Saudi Arabia announced it had resumed flights there. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, slipped below $115 a barrel after jumping above $117 on Friday on fears that more fighting in the Middle East could disrupt energy markets.

One of the biggest names in Big Law appears to be wobbling.

Days after the legal heavyweights Weil Gotshal & Manges and Willkie Farr & Gallagher broke off talks to merge, reports have emerged of more potential partner departures at Weil Gotshal, Elizabeth Olson reports.

Costly defections: Among the high-powered partners who may leave is Ramona Nee, a managing partner. She was set to lead the partnership in January but has decided against it, according to The Financial Times and other publications.

Nee, who has decades of deal-making experience, has had discussions about joining Simpson Thacher & Bartlett, a global firm based in New York City, Semafor reported. A number of star lawyers have exited Weil Gotshal already, but Nee’s departure is not certain.

The stakes are high. The 1,200-lawyer firm had gross revenues of $2 billion in 2024 from its restructuring, corporate law and complex litigation work. If it fails to find a merger partner, it could opt for bankruptcy. That would create one of the biggest firm collapses since Dewey & LeBoeuf shut down in 2012.

Weil Gotshal has been a force in restructuring. The firm, founded in 1931, led historic bankruptcies for companies including Lehman Brothers, Enron and WorldCom. But its revenue growth hasn’t kept pace with big rivals’ in recent years.

Its troubles come amid intensifying competition for top lawyers. In the competition for rainmakers, firms are offering compensation of as much as $35 million annually, leading more lawyers to abandon the tradition of staying with one firm for their entire careers.

Quote of the day

Katie Porter, a progressive former Democratic congresswoman from California, on her state’s proposed billionaire tax, which she opposes. The debate over the ballot measure has helped forge atypical political alliances, as many unions have sided with the ultrarich against the tax over questions about how the revenue would be spent. Another concern: Would it drive the state’s high earners away and harm major capital projects?

The White House has shown a willingness to cut business deals with Russia even as it seeks to end the war Moscow started in Ukraine.

This month, President Trump announced an agreement with President Vladimir Putin of Russia that would ease sanctions on the country in exchange for the release of Russian diesel fuel to the global market.

Now, another proposed U.S.-Russia energy deal is drawing scrutiny — and underscoring the pitfalls of mixing business and diplomacy in wartime.

Last month, Trump’s peace envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, discussed a plan with Putin in which a purported U.S. company called Polar LNG would buy Russian technology and use it to produce and export natural gas from Alaska, according to The Times:

But it turns out that the company was not an all-American affair. The multibillion-dollar project has received secret funding from the same powerful Russian company that was to provide the technology, according to the energy executive who until last month led the U.S. firm and two others involved in company negotiations.

Joel Riddle, who was chief executive of the company, Polar LNG, until he resigned in September, said he had been misled about the sources of the start-up funding, which ostensibly came from a company in the United Arab Emirates.

Instead, Mr. Riddle said he learned the true source of at least some of Polar LNG’s money was Novatek, a Russian energy giant under partial U.S. sanctions.

“It’s not only unlawful, but it’s not in the U.S. interest to have Russian technology controlling the commercialization of Arctic gas in the North Slope,” Mr. Riddle said in a brief interview.

Novatek said in a statement to The Times that it was moving to acquire “minority shareholder” status in the Polar LNG project.

Deals

item.title: Meta and SpaceX to Raise Billions More to Fund A.I. Ambitions
item.description:
As the tech industry faces questions about the huge spending on infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence, some of the largest companies are raising tens of billions of dollars to drive their ambitions.

On Monday morning, Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, announced it could raise up to $95 billion from selling stock. Shortly after, SpaceX, the A.I. and rocket company led by Elon Musk, said it had closed a $40 billion debt round to pay for the chips it needed for its data centers.

The two announcements come ahead of the planned initial public offering of Anthropic, the A.I. behemoth behind the Claude chatbot, which is expected later this year and could further compete for investor interest. The company unveiled financial figures on Monday, paving the way for an offering that could aim to raise more than $100 billion in what may be the world’s largest I.P.O.

In a financial disclosure earlier this month, Meta acknowledged the competitive market, and said it would be “prudent” to raise more money “before even more companies have absorbed available capital.”

“Recent significant capital raises at other notable companies, and others soon anticipated to take place, to fund the same A.I. growth — for example, Alphabet, SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI — have resulted in an increasingly challenging environment for raising capital,” the company said in the filing.

Meta, SpaceX and others are all spending billions of dollars in a global race to dominate A.I., building massive data centers and buying up chips to power the technology. But the spending has also caused some jitters in the market, with technology stocks largely falling in the past month.

Meta declined to comment. SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The financing announced by Meta on Monday includes a $35 billion stock offering, as well as the sale of another $60 billion in non-voting shares. Earlier this month, the company said it would create a class of non-voting shares that would help it raise capital, compensate employees and aid in potential acquisitions, while preserving the majority control over shareholder decision-making enjoyed by its chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg.

Meta said in its announcement that chipmakers including Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom had indicated interest in purchasing a total of $5 billion in the stock offering. Critics have previously raised concerns about this type of circular financing, as chipmakers, A.I. labs and computing providers that do business together have also invested in or lent money to one another, deeply intertwining their financial fates.

SpaceX raised $40 billion to lease equipment for data centers and called it “the largest committed” financing for A.I. chips, the company said in a news release. SpaceX uses its data centers to power its own A.I. model, Grok, and leases some of its other compute capacity to other A.I. companies including Google and Anthropic.

Lead investors in the deal include Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which also advised in structuring the deal, SpaceX said. Other investors include includes BlackRock and certain accounts advised by KKR.

On Sunday, Mr. Musk hinted at future pain for so-called neocloud organizations, which build data centers to then lease computing power to A.I. firm, in a post on his social media platform X.

“As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers,” Mr. Musk wrote, predicting a near future of failure and consolidation for some of the companies.

item.title: DraftKings Faces Growing Pressure Over How It Targets Customers
item.description:
DraftKings and other online gambling companies are facing mounting scrutiny as federal lawmakers and officials in several states have begun questioning them in recent weeks about their use of artificial intelligence and behavioral data to keep their customers betting.

In New York, consumer protection lawyers from the attorney general’s office have contacted former DraftKings employees to discuss the company’s data practices, according to three former employees who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a confidential inquiry or out of fear of retaliation, and messages reviewed by The New York Times. At the same time, the state’s gaming commission has proposed sharp limits on how operators can deploy A.I.

In Louisiana, gambling regulators voted to delay a routine license renewal for DraftKings, partly to allow themselves time to investigate how the company uses A.I. and customer data.

And in Congress, three lawmakers sent letters last week to online gambling companies, including DraftKings, requesting details about their “V.I.P.” programs and their use of A.I.

The actions follow reporting from The Times in September that found DraftKings had deployed machine learning, a form of artificial intelligence that seeks patterns in data, to analyze customer records and identify those most likely to continue gambling and losing when sent promotions. Former employees who built those systems told The Times that they worried the technology would harm gamblers struggling with addiction. Regulators in Massachusetts and Michigan announced shortly afterward that they were looking into the issue.

DraftKings “does not use artificial intelligence to target customers based on losses and does not market to customers based on indicators of potential problem gaming,” a spokesperson said in a statement, adding that the company “values an open and ongoing dialogue with regulators” and that “regular conversations and check-ins with regulators are normal course of business.”

Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and two other Democrats, Representatives Paul Tonko of New York and Valerie Foushee of North Carolina, published their letters to DraftKings and five other companies late last week, demanding a response by Nov. 5.

They cited The Times’s findings as well as recent reporting by ProPublica, which found that DraftKings granted V.I.P. status to a reporter deliberately mimicking signs of problem gambling, and other articles about online gambling by the Philadelphia Inquirer and The Guardian.

“Sportsbooks are supercharging addiction, using A.I. to target users and keep them hooked on gambling,” Mr. Blumenthal told The Times in a statement.

Lawyers from the New York attorney general’s office have been asking former DraftKings employees about issues raised by The Times’s story, the three former employees said. The lawyers work for the Bureau of Consumer Frauds and Protection, as well as the Bureau of Internet and Technology, which has recently led high-profile lawsuits against social media giants, including Meta and TikTok, over addictive algorithms.

The extent of their inquiry remains unclear. The attorney general’s office declined to comment on the matter.

Separately, the New York State Gaming Commission announced this month that it had unanimously voted to propose regulations that would effectively bar gambling companies from using automated systems to target customers with personalized promotions, or from suggesting wagers based on their betting history or losses.

The proposed rule will undergo a 60-day public comment period, possible revisions and a final vote before taking effect. It expands on a brief initial version that regulators released for feedback in March, which drew pushback from DraftKings and other major sports betting companies. In written comments in May, DraftKings argued that the proposal could result in “broad restrictions on legitimate business uses of A.I.” and that the technology had the potential to “improve the customer experience.”

Brian O’Dwyer, the commission’s chairman, said in a statement that while legalized sports betting has brought New York billions in tax revenue since it legalized the practice in 2022, it can still pose a danger.

“I don’t believe anyone gave real long-term consideration of how quickly technology could be developed and used to extract as much money as possible from unsuspecting individuals,” he said.

In Louisiana, the state’s gaming control board voted this month to hold up a standard five-year license renewal for DraftKings and place the company on a four-month conditional extension instead.

The board ordered DraftKings to answer formal questions from its investigators about its use of A.I., and to submit overdue paperwork. DraftKings’ spokesperson said the board was allowing the company “additional time” to complete its application, which is “common in such administrative matters.”

The order happened during an Oct. 15 hearing in Baton Rouge in which the board grilled two DraftKings executives. Christopher Hebert, the board’s chairman, said that The Times’s report raised “serious questions.”

Paul Liberman, a DraftKings co-founder and president, acknowledged that DraftKings had the ability to track winners and losers, but denied that the company was singling out losing bettors.

“Most customers that play on the platform are not going to be winners,” Mr. Liberman told the board. He added that he preferred the phrase “spending money” — rather than losing money — because customers were paying for entertainment.

Bianca Pallaro, Jenny Vrentas and Walt Bogdanich contributed reporting.
